title: Bayesian Inference
tagline: How to change your mind by exactly the right amount.
description: From probability-as-belief to posterior distributions. Every concept is gated: you advance when the evidence says you know it.

intro.hook: A rule for changing your mind by exactly the right amount, no more and no less.
body: You already reason this way, badly. You hold a belief, evidence arrives, you update. The trouble is that human updating is systematically wrong in known directions: we ignore how rare things are to begin with, and we treat weak evidence as strong.

Bayes' theorem is the arithmetic of doing it correctly. It says precisely how much a piece of evidence should move you, given how likely that evidence was under each explanation — and given what you believed before it arrived.

The famous consequence is that a 99%-accurate test for a rare disease can still leave you far more likely healthy than sick. That is not a trick or a paradox. It is what happens when you finally account for the base rate, and it is the moment most people realise their intuition needs an upgrade.

why.title: Uncertainty is the normal case
why.text: Diagnosis, forecasting, search, spam filtering and scientific inference are all decisions under incomplete information.

why.title: It names your assumptions
why.text: The prior forces you to state what you believed beforehand. That is the feature — hidden assumptions are the dangerous ones.

why.title: It fixes a real bug in your head
why.text: Base-rate neglect is measurable, widespread, and expensive. This is the correction.

intro.closer: Bayes never published it. A friend found the essay among his papers after he died.

concepts.title: Probability as degree of belief
concepts.summary: A probability can measure how strongly you believe something, on a 0-to-1 scale, and beliefs must obey the rules of probability to be coherent.

cards.h: Two readings of the same number
cards.md:
Say a weather app shows **70% chance of rain**. There is only one tomorrow — it will either rain or it won't. So what is the 70% *about*?

The **frequentist** reading: probability is a long-run frequency. Across many days *like* tomorrow, it rains on 70% of them.

The **Bayesian** reading: probability is a **degree of belief**. 70% measures how confident the forecaster is about *this* tomorrow, given everything known right now.

Both readings use identical math. Bayesian inference simply takes the belief reading seriously — which lets you put probabilities on one-off things: this trade, this diagnosis, this hypothesis.

Degrees of belief live on a 0-to-1 scale:

- **0** — certain it's false
- **0.5** — maximally unsure (for a yes/no question)
- **1** — certain it's true

A belief of 0.9 isn't a vibe; it's a commitment. It says you'd judge 9:1 odds as fair. If you *say* 0.9 but would only bet at even odds, your stated belief and your real belief disagree — and the real one is the one at 0.5.

Beliefs can be anything you like — except self-contradictory. If you believe *rain* at 0.7, you must believe *no rain* at 0.3. If your beliefs violate the probability rules, a bookie can construct a set of bets you'd accept individually that guarantee you lose money (a *Dutch book*).

That's the whole foundation: **Bayesian inference is the accounting system that keeps beliefs coherent as evidence arrives.** Everything that follows is bookkeeping done correctly.

questions.prompt: A Bayesian says 'the probability this startup succeeds is 20%.' What does the 20% measure?
options: The fraction of similar startups that succeed
Their degree of belief that this startup succeeds, given current information
Nothing — one-off events can't have probabilities
feedback: That's the frequentist reading — reference-class frequency. A Bayesian can use that as an input, but the 20% itself is about belief in this case.
Right. It quantifies confidence about this specific case given what's known now.
There's no separate 'objective rate' living inside a one-off event — that's the point the belief reading solves.
Backwards — putting probabilities on one-off events is exactly what the belief interpretation permits.

questions.prompt: You believe P(market up tomorrow) = 0.6. Coherence requires your P(market not up) to be:
feedback: Beliefs are personal but not lawless — they must sum correctly or you're Dutch-bookable.
Then P(up) + P(not up) = 1.2 — incoherent; you'd accept a guaranteed-loss set of bets.
Correct: complements must sum to 1. That's the minimum price of coherence.
Coherence is about your beliefs now, not the outcome later.

questions.prompt: Which claim is a *Bayesian* probability statement that a strict frequentist would refuse to make?
options: This coin lands heads 50% of flips in the long run
About 1% of these parts are defective
There's a 75% probability this specific hypothesis is true
The die shows a 6 on 1/6 of rolls
feedback: Long-run frequency — fully frequentist.
A population rate — frequentist territory.
Yes. A hypothesis is either true or false; only the belief interpretation lets you put 75% on it.
Long-run frequency again.

concepts.title: Joint and conditional probability
concepts.summary: P(A|B) is belief in A after learning B. The product rule P(A and B) = P(A|B)P(B) ties joint, conditional, and marginal beliefs together.

cards.md:
P(A) is your belief in A knowing nothing special. **P(A | B)** — 'probability of A *given* B' — is your belief in A *after learning B is true*.

Example: P(a random person is over 6 ft) might be 0.15. P(over 6 ft | plays pro basketball) is much higher. Same person-property, different information state.

Conditioning is not a minor notation. It is *the* operation of learning. All of Bayesian inference is: **condition your beliefs on what you observed.**

The joint probability that two things are both true factors cleanly:

**P(A and B) = P(A | B) × P(B)**

Read it as a story: for both to hold, first B happens (P(B)), then A happens *in a world where B is true* (P(A|B)).

It factors the other way too: P(A and B) = P(B | A) × P(A).

Those two factorizations describe the same joint quantity — hold that thought; setting them equal is where Bayes' theorem (the rule for reversing a conditional) comes from.

**P(A|B) is not P(B|A).** The probability a person is a pro basketball player *given* they're over 6 ft is tiny; the probability they're over 6 ft *given* they're pro is huge.

Confusing the two is called the *inverse fallacy*, and it's not academic: prosecutors have argued 'P(evidence | innocent) is tiny, so P(innocent | evidence) is tiny.' Those are different numbers, and the gap between them is exactly what Bayes' theorem computes.

questions.prompt: P(cloudy) = 0.4 and P(rain | cloudy) = 0.5. P(cloudy and rain) = ?
feedback: You added. The product rule multiplies: joint = conditional × marginal.
That's just P(rain|cloudy); you still need to weight by how likely 'cloudy' is.
Check the arithmetic: 0.5 × 0.4.

questions.prompt: Roughly 90% of spam emails contain a link. Can you conclude that ~90% of emails containing a link are spam?
options: No — that reverses the conditional, and P(spam|link) depends on how common spam and links are overall
Yes, if the sample is large
No, because 90% is too high to be real
feedback: P(link|spam) and P(spam|link) are different quantities.
Exactly. Plenty of legitimate email contains links; the reversed conditional needs base rates.
Sample size doesn't fix a reversed conditional.
The number's size is irrelevant; the direction of the conditional is the issue.

questions.prompt: Which expression equals P(A and B)?
feedback: Addition is for 'or' (and only for exclusive events).
Conditionals don't add into a joint.
Yes — the product rule, factored through A.
Only when A and B are independent. The product rule holds always; this shortcut doesn't.

concepts.title: Bayes' theorem
concepts.summary: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E). It is the product rule rearranged — the rule for reversing a conditional legally.

cards.md:
From the last concept, the joint factors both ways:

P(H and E) = P(H|E)·P(E) = P(E|H)·P(H)

Divide both sides by P(E):

## P(H|E) = P(E|H) · P(H) / P(E)

That's the entire theorem. Nothing mystical — it's the product rule rearranged. Its power is *direction*: it converts the conditional you can usually compute, P(evidence | hypothesis), into the one you actually want, P(hypothesis | evidence).

Models naturally run forward: *if* the coin is fair, *then* P(3 heads) is easy. *If* the patient has the disease, *then* P(positive test) is in the test's spec sheet.

But you observe the evidence and want the hypothesis: P(fair | 3 heads), P(disease | positive). Bayes' theorem is the legal move from forward to backward — the inverse fallacy done right, with P(H) and P(E) supplying exactly the correction the fallacy omits.

P(E) — the total probability of the evidence — is computed by summing over all the ways E could happen:

P(E) = P(E|H)·P(H) + P(E|not H)·P(not H)

It's the *normalizer*: it makes the posteriors (the updated beliefs after evidence) across all hypotheses sum to 1. A useful instinct: evidence that is likely under many hypotheses (big P(E)) moves you little; evidence that is *only* likely under one hypothesis moves you a lot.

questions.prompt: P(H) = 0.5, P(E|H) = 0.8, P(E|not H) = 0.4. What is P(H|E)?
feedback: 0.8 is P(E|H) — the forward direction, not the answer.
That's the numerator 0.8×0.5 without normalizing by P(E).
The evidence favored H 2:1 — the belief must move off 0.5.

questions.prompt: In P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E), what job does P(E) do?
options: Measures how good the hypothesis is
Normalizes, so posteriors over all hypotheses sum to 1
It's a fudge factor chosen to get the answer you want
feedback: Hypothesis quality lives in P(E|H) and P(H).
Correct — it's total probability of the evidence across all hypotheses.
It's fully determined by the model: sum P(E|Hᵢ)P(Hᵢ).
Only if H were certain. In general P(E) averages over all hypotheses.

questions.prompt: Evidence E is almost equally likely whether H is true or false. What does observing E do to your belief in H?
feedback: Strong confirmation needs P(E|H) >> P(E|not H).
Refutation needs the reverse asymmetry.
Right — uninformative evidence, ratio near 1, posterior ≈ prior.
The posterior stays near the *prior*, wherever that was — not at 0.5.

concepts.title: Prior, likelihood, posterior
concepts.summary: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The prior is belief before data, the likelihood scores hypotheses by how well they predict the data, the posterior is belief after.

cards.md:
Bayes' theorem, with its parts named:

**posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence**

- **Prior** P(H): belief before this data arrived
- **Likelihood** P(E|H): how well hypothesis H predicts the observed data — *a function of H*, with the data held fixed
- **Posterior** P(H|E): belief after
- **Evidence** P(E): the normalizer

Because the normalizer doesn't depend on H, the working form is:

## posterior ∝ likelihood × prior

cards.h: The likelihood is not a probability over hypotheses
cards.md:
Subtle but load-bearing: the likelihood asks, for each candidate hypothesis, *'how surprised would this hypothesis be by the data I actually saw?'*

Fix the data. Vary the hypothesis. The resulting scores don't need to sum to 1 — they're not a distribution over hypotheses, they're a *scorecard*. Hypotheses that predicted the data well score high; hypotheses that would have been shocked score low.

The posterior then blends that scorecard with the prior.

Each part has one job:

- The **prior** carries everything you knew *before* — base rates, past results, structure.
- The **likelihood** carries everything the *new data* says.
- The **posterior** is their product, renormalized.

Neither part is optional. Data without priors ignores what you already knew (see the next concept for how badly that goes); priors without data is just stubbornness. The posterior is the negotiated settlement — and it's tomorrow's prior.

questions.prompt: You flip a coin 10 times and see 7 heads. In evaluating 'this coin is fair,' the number P(7 heads in 10 | fair) ≈ 0.117 is the:
feedback: The prior is your belief in fairness before flipping.
Right — data fixed, hypothesis assumed, it scores how well 'fair' predicts what you saw.
The posterior is P(fair | 7 heads) — it also needs the prior and normalizer.
The evidence averages over all hypotheses, not just 'fair.'

questions.prompt: Why can we write posterior ∝ likelihood × prior, dropping P(E)?
options: P(E) doesn't depend on which hypothesis you're scoring, so it rescales all posteriors equally
feedback: P(E) is rarely 1.
Correct — it's a common denominator across hypotheses; relative belief is unaffected, and you can renormalize at the end.
It's computable — sum likelihood×prior over hypotheses. It's just not needed for comparing them.
It's exact, not approximate; normalization is deferred, not lost.

questions.prompt: Likelihood values across all candidate hypotheses sum to 1.4. Is something wrong?
options: No — the likelihood is a function of the hypothesis, not a distribution over hypotheses
Yes — the data must be corrupted
No — but only because 1.4 is close to 1
feedback: The likelihood isn't a probability distribution over H. Each value is a probability *of the data*, under a different H.
Exactly. It's a scorecard, not a distribution; no sum-to-1 constraint applies.
Nothing about the data is implicated.
The sum could be 0.03 or 12 — any value is fine.

concepts.title: The diagnostic test: base rates bite
concepts.summary: With a rare condition, even an accurate test yields mostly false positives. The prior (base rate) dominates when evidence is moderate.

cards.md:
A disease affects **1 in 1,000** people. A test catches 99% of true cases (sensitivity) and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people (false-positive rate).

You test positive. What's the probability you have the disease?

Most people — including most physicians in published studies (Casscells 1978, and replications since) — answer near 95%. Lock in your own answer before the next card.

Skip the formula; count 100,000 people.

- Sick: 100. Of these, **99** test positive.
- Healthy: 99,900. Of these, 5% — **4,995** — test positive.

Positives total 99 + 4,995 = 5,094. True positives: 99.

## P(disease | positive) = 99 / 5,094 ≈ 1.9%

Not 95%. The false positives outnumber the true ones 50-to-1, because the healthy population is enormous. The 'accurate test' intuition ignored the prior.

This is base-rate neglect, and it's the single most consequential Bayesian error in the wild — medicine, fraud detection, security alerts, trading signals.

The pattern: **when the prior is extreme, moderate evidence cannot overcome it.** A 20:1 likelihood ratio (how strongly evidence favors one side) applied to a 1-in-1000 prior still leaves you overwhelmingly likely healthy.

Corollary for any alert system: if the condition you're screening for is rare, most alerts are false — no matter how good the detector looks on paper. The fix is either a stronger detector or a second, independent test (next concept).

questions.prompt: Same test (99% sensitivity, 5% false positives), but the disease affects 1 in 10 people. Roughly what is P(disease | positive)?
feedback: That was the 1-in-1000 answer; the prior is now 100× larger.
Recount: per 1,000 people — 100 sick → 99 positive; 900 healthy → 45 positive.
Right: 99/(99+45) ≈ 69%. Same test, different prior, wildly different posterior.
Even at a 10% base rate, false positives still drag it well below 99%.

questions.prompt: Your fraud model flags transactions with a 1% false-positive rate and 95% detection. Fraud is 1 in 10,000 transactions. Of flagged transactions, roughly what fraction are actually fraud?
feedback: That's the detector's spec, not the posterior.
The base rate is far too low for a coin-flip posterior.
Close — but compute it: per 1M txns, 95 true flags vs ~10,000 false flags.
Yes: 95/(95+9,999) ≈ 0.9%. Over 99% of flags are false. Rare condition + moderate evidence = alert fatigue.

questions.prompt: What single change most efficiently rescues the rare-disease test's posterior?
options: Cut the false-positive rate from 5% toward 0.1%
feedback: Sensitivity barely matters here — the 99 true positives weren't the problem; the 4,995 false ones were.
Right. False positives dominate the denominator; cutting them 50× lifts the posterior from ~2% to ~50%.
More tests scale both counts equally.
Precision of reporting doesn't touch the math.

concepts.title: Sequential updating
concepts.summary: Today's posterior is tomorrow's prior. Independent evidence can be absorbed piece by piece, in any order, and lands on the same posterior.

cards.md:
Bayes' theorem isn't a one-shot formula — it's a **loop**:

1. Hold a prior.
2. Observe evidence.
3. Compute the posterior.
4. **That posterior is your new prior.** Go to 2.

This is why Bayesian inference fits streaming reality — markets, sensors, test results. You never start over; every belief you hold is the compressed summary of everything you've seen so far.

If two pieces of evidence are independent given the hypothesis, you can process E₁ then E₂, or E₂ then E₁, or both at once — the final posterior is identical. Multiplication commutes:

posterior ∝ P(E₂|H) · P(E₁|H) · prior

This is a powerful sanity check: if your updating procedure gives different answers depending on the order you read the news, it isn't Bayesian — something is leaking.

The loop has one failure mode worth tattooing somewhere: **evidence may be counted once.**

If two news stories both trace back to the same source, they are one piece of evidence wearing two hats. Updating on both is like flipping a coin once and recording it twice. Correlated signals — analysts quoting each other, indicators derived from the same price series — must be discounted or your posterior becomes confident far beyond what the world actually told you.

cards.h: A lab panel is not three pieces of evidence
cards.md:
The condition has a name worth knowing: evidence must be **conditionally independent** — independent *given the hypothesis*. Not merely "different measurements", and not "uncorrelated in the population".

A standard lipid panel is the trap. Total cholesterol, LDL and non-HDL are largely **re-expressions of overlapping measurements** — non-HDL is total minus HDL by definition. Suppose each carries a likelihood ratio of 3 for elevated cardiac risk, against a 10% pre-test probability:

## naive: 1:9 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3:1 → **75%**

Treat them honestly as close to one measurement and it is 1:9 × 3 = 1:3, or **25%**. Same patient, same numbers, same afternoon — and a difference that changes what you do.

The tell is mechanical, not statistical: ask what each marker is *made of*. Two quantities computed from the same blood draw, one partly by subtraction from the other, cannot be three independent votes.

questions.prompt: After updating on this morning's data, your posterior for a hypothesis is 0.7. New independent data arrives this afternoon. What prior do you use?
options: The original prior from last week
feedback: Re-using the old prior throws away this morning's evidence.
Resetting to neutral erases everything you learned.
Right — posterior in, prior out. The chain is the whole method.
Choosing to reach a conclusion isn't inference; it's motivated reasoning.

questions.prompt: Three independent studies each favor a drug with likelihood ratio 2:1. Processed sequentially from a 1:1 prior, the final odds are:
feedback: That's one study's worth.
You added the ratios; independent evidence multiplies.
Yes: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8:1. Independent likelihood ratios multiply.
Multiplication commutes — order can't matter for independent evidence.

questions.prompt: Five financial newsletters all turn bearish the same week, and all five cite the same bank's report. As evidence, this is closest to:
options: Five independent updates — strong bear signal
Roughly one update — the newsletters are correlated through their source
Zero updates — newsletters are never evidence
feedback: Counting them separately double- (quintuple-) counts one report.
Right. One underlying source ≈ one piece of evidence; the echoes add almost nothing.
The underlying report is real evidence — once.
Bayes says discount the echo, not invert it; contrarianism needs its own evidence.

questions.prompt: A cardiology risk tool multiplies likelihood ratios from total cholesterol, LDL and non-HDL cholesterol, treating each as separate evidence. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The posterior risk is overstated, because the three markers are largely the same measurement
The posterior risk is understated, because correlated evidence cancels
No effect — likelihood ratios always multiply
The result is fine as long as each likelihood ratio was measured accurately
feedback: Correct. Non-HDL is total minus HDL by definition, so this is close to counting one measurement three times. On a 10% pre-test probability with LR 3 each, the naive answer is 75% against roughly 25% — the newsletter error in a white coat.
Correlated evidence does not cancel; it over-accumulates. Each repetition pushes the odds the same way, so the error is confident overshoot rather than dilution.
They multiply only when the pieces are conditionally independent — independent given the hypothesis. That is a real assumption about the world, not a property of the arithmetic.
Accuracy per marker is not the issue. Each LR can be perfectly measured in isolation and the combination still be wrong, because the error is in treating them as separate votes.

concepts.title: Odds form and Bayes factors
concepts.summary: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The Bayes factor cleanly separates what the evidence says from what you believed before.

cards.md:
Odds are just probability in ratio clothing: p = 0.75 is odds of 3:1 (0.75/0.25). Odds of 1:4 is p = 0.2.

Why bother? Because in odds form, Bayes' theorem loses its denominator entirely:

## posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio

where the **likelihood ratio** (or **Bayes factor**) is P(E|H) / P(E|not H) — how many times better the hypothesis predicts the evidence than its rival.

The Bayes factor is the cleanest possible answer to *'what does this evidence actually say?'* — fully separated from your prior.

- LR (likelihood ratio) = 20 — strong evidence for H
- LR = 1 — the evidence says nothing
- LR = 0.05 — strong evidence against H

Redo the diagnostic test instantly: prior odds 1:999, LR = 0.99/0.05 ≈ 20. Posterior odds = 20:999 ≈ 1:50 → about 2%. Same answer as the town-counting, three seconds of arithmetic.

Take logs and multiplication becomes addition: each independent piece of evidence *adds* its log-likelihood-ratio to your running log-odds. Evidence becomes an additive currency — 'this signal is worth +3 decibans, that one −1.'

This is how spam filters score messages, and how Alan Turing's team at Bletchley weighed Enigma evidence (they coined the *ban*). When you hear 'weight of evidence,' this is the literal weighing.

questions.prompt: Prior odds 1:4 that a strategy has real edge. A backtest result has likelihood ratio 8 in its favor. Posterior odds — and roughly posterior probability?
feedback: You multiplied the wrong side — LR of 8 favors the hypothesis.
You added; odds form multiplies.
That ignores the 1:4 prior.

questions.prompt: A Bayes factor of exactly 1 means:
options: The evidence is equally probable under both hypotheses — it moves nothing
feedback: The posterior equals the *prior*, which can be anything — not necessarily 50%.
Correct. Multiply odds by 1: no change. Uninformative evidence.
Proof would be LR → ∞.
The BF says nothing about the prior; that's exactly its virtue.

questions.prompt: Two independent signals have likelihood ratios 10 and 0.1. Net effect on your odds:
feedback: The 0.1 exactly undoes the 10.
Symmetric reasoning — the 10 undoes the 0.1.
Right: 10 × 0.1 = 1. In log-odds, +1 and −1 sum to zero.
Independent LRs multiply — that's the core mechanic of this concept.

concepts.title: Continuous beliefs: the Beta-Binomial
concepts.summary: For an unknown rate, the belief is a whole distribution over [0,1]. Beta(a,b) updates on heads/tails by simply incrementing a or b.

cards.md:
So far our hypotheses were discrete: sick/healthy, edge/no-edge. But 'what fraction of the time does this coin land heads?' has a *continuum* of hypotheses — every value of θ between 0 and 1.

A Bayesian's belief about θ is therefore a **whole curve**: a probability density over [0,1]. Tall where you think θ likely lives, flat where you're unsure. Updating reshapes the entire curve at once — every candidate θ gets multiplied by how well it predicted the data.

The workhorse curve for rates is **Beta(a, b)**. Read its two parameters as *pseudo-counts*:

- Beta(1, 1) — flat; total ignorance about θ
- Beta(5, 5) — probably near 0.5
- Beta(20, 4) — probably near 0.83

Mean ≈ a/(a+b). Bigger a+b = more (pseudo-)data = tighter curve. The prior literally says: 'I walk in as if I'd already seen a−1 heads and b−1 tails.'

Here's the payoff. If your prior is Beta(a, b) and you observe h heads and t tails:

## posterior = Beta(a + h, b + t)

That's it. The full Bayes machinery — likelihood times prior, normalize the curve — collapses to *incrementing two counters*. This happy algebra is called **conjugacy** (the Beta is conjugate to the Binomial — the distribution of heads in n flips), and it's why Beta-Binomial models run in production everywhere: A/B tests, click-through rates, win rates.

questions.prompt: Prior Beta(2, 2) on a coin's heads-rate. You flip 10 times: 7 heads, 3 tails. Posterior?
feedback: You dropped the prior's pseudo-counts.
Right: (2+7, 2+3). Add heads to a, tails to b.
Counts add; they don't multiply.
Whole observations add as whole counts.

questions.prompt: Two analysts model a click-through rate: one starts from Beta(1,1), the other from Beta(60,140). After both see the same 1,000,000 impressions, their posteriors are:
options: Nearly identical — a million observations swamp 200 pseudo-counts
feedback: Destiny only when data is scarce.
Right. Posterior counts are ~prior + 1,000,000; the prior's contribution is a rounding error. Data swamps the prior.
A million observations reshape any finite prior.
Same model, same data — directly comparable.

questions.prompt: Beta(21, 3) versus Beta(7, 1) have the same mean (0.875). What differs?
options: Beta(21, 3) is tighter: more pseudo-data, more confidence around that mean
Only the mean matters in Bayesian inference
feedback: A belief is the whole curve, not its mean.
Right — a+b = 24 vs 8. Same center, three times the effective evidence, visibly narrower curve.
Fewer pseudo-counts = wider, not tighter.
Two beliefs with equal means can imply very different bets; the spread is the risk.

concepts.title: Choosing priors
concepts.summary: Priors encode pre-data knowledge. Flat isn't neutral, informative priors are honest when defensible, and sensitivity analysis is the discipline that keeps them safe.

cards.md:
'Priors are subjective — you can get any answer you want.' This is the standard objection to Bayes, and it deserves a straight response:

1. *Everyone* has priors; Bayesians just write theirs down where they can be criticized.
2. With reasonable data, priors wash out (you proved this in the last checkpoint).
3. When priors *don't* wash out — small data, rare events — that is precisely when pretending you don't have one causes disasters like the base-rate fallacy.

A tempting dodge: 'use a flat prior and stay objective.' But flat in one parameterization is curved in another — flat on θ is *not* flat on θ², or on log-odds of θ. Every prior takes a stance; flatness just hides which one.

Practical guidance:
- **Weakly informative** priors (broad but not absurd) are the modern default — they rule out the ridiculous without steering the answer.
- **Informative** priors are correct when you genuinely have prior evidence — last quarter's rates, published effect sizes, physical limits. Discarding known information is not humility; it's waste.

The professional discipline that makes priors safe: **rerun the analysis under several defensible priors.**

- Conclusions agree → the data is doing the work; report with confidence.
- Conclusions diverge → the data is too weak to decide, and *that is the finding*. Report the divergence; collect more data.

A Bayesian result quoted without sensitivity checks is a single scenario, not an analysis.

questions.prompt: A colleague: 'I used a flat prior, so my analysis is assumption-free.' The sharpest correction:
options: Flat on one scale is informative on another; the assumption is hidden, not absent
feedback: Flat-on-θ is a specific stance that transforms into a non-flat stance on other scales.
Right. Every prior takes a position; flatness just obscures which one.
Flat priors are often fine — the claim of assumption-freedom is what's wrong.
They matter exactly when data is thin.

questions.prompt: Estimating the failure rate of a new part, when three prior generations of the same part all failed at 1-3%. The best prior:
options: Flat on [0,1] — new part, blank slate
Weakly concentrated near 1-3% but with real spread — use the history, stay open to surprise
Whatever makes the new part look best
feedback: Ignoring three generations of directly relevant data is waste, not objectivity.
Right — informative but honest. History in, dogma out.
A point mass can never update; it's certainty, not belief.
That's advocacy. Bayes is accounting, not marketing.

questions.prompt: Under three defensible priors your conclusion flips sign. The Bayesian response:
options: Report the prior whose answer you prefer
Average the three answers and report that
Report that the data cannot yet decide, and gather more
feedback: Prior-shopping is the one sin the framework cannot survive.
An average of divergent scenarios manufactures false confidence.
Right. Divergence under sensitivity analysis IS the result: insufficient evidence.
The divergence was a discovery, not a failure — a non-Bayesian analysis would simply have hidden it.

concepts.title: From posterior to decision
concepts.summary: The posterior is the input, not the output: predictions integrate over it, and decisions maximize expected utility under it. Capstone concept.

cards.h: Prediction: average over what you don't know
cards.md:
What's the probability the *next* flip is heads? Not 'the best θ' — you don't know θ. The **posterior predictive** averages the prediction over every candidate θ, weighted by your posterior belief in it.

For Beta(a, b) it's beautifully simple: P(next is heads) = a/(a+b). With posterior Beta(9,5): 9/14 ≈ 0.64.

The honest prediction bakes in your *uncertainty about the rate*, not just the rate's best guess.

A posterior alone never tells you what to do — you also need what each outcome *costs*. The rule: **choose the action with the best expected utility (probability-weighted value) under the posterior.**

A 2% posterior of disease sounds dismissible — until the follow-up test costs $50 and the missed disease is fatal; then 2% commands action. A 60% posterior of trading edge sounds actionable — until the downside is ruin. Same posteriors, opposite decisions, because the payoffs differ. Probabilities and payoffs are separate inputs; Bayes owns the first, you must supply the second.

cards.h: The whole method on one card
cards.md:
You now hold the complete loop:

1. **Prior** — write down what you believe and why.
2. **Likelihood** — model how each hypothesis predicts data.
3. **Update** — posterior ∝ likelihood × prior (odds form for speed; conjugate forms when lucky).
4. **Check** — sensitivity analysis across defensible priors.
5. **Predict & decide** — posterior predictive for forecasts; expected utility for actions.
6. **Loop** — today's posterior is tomorrow's prior.

The mastery review will now interleave everything. That's not ceremony — spaced, mixed retrieval is where retention is actually built.

questions.prompt: Posterior on a conversion rate: Beta(30, 70). The honest probability that the next visitor converts:
feedback: Right: a/(a+b) = 30/100. The posterior predictive collapses to the posterior mean here.
That's b's share — the non-conversion side.
Averaging over the posterior is exactly how you predict *without* knowing the true rate.

questions.prompt: Alarm A: posterior 0.9 of a trivial fault costing $10. Alarm B: posterior 0.02 of a failure costing $100,000. Which does a Bayesian decision-maker investigate first?
feedback: Probability alone isn't a decision rule.
Right. 0.02 × 100,000 = 2,000 ≫ 0.9 × 10 = 9. Consequences weight the posterior.
Certainty thresholds are for mastery gates, not loss management.
The expected losses differ by 200×; this is not a coin-flip situation.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is the Bayesian workflow in the right order?
options: Decide → collect data → choose the prior that supports the decision
Prior → likelihood → posterior → sensitivity check → predict/decide
feedback: That's the workflow of motivated reasoning, formalized.
Right — belief in, evidence weighed, belief out, stress-tested, then acted on.
The prior can't come last; it means 'before.'
The arrow of the method runs prior → posterior, never backward.

preface.hook: A test that is right 99% of the time just said you have a rare disease. The chance you actually have it can still be small.
body: That sounds like a trick, and it is not. Suppose one person in ten thousand has some illness, and the test is right 99 times out of 100.

Test a million people. About a hundred of them genuinely have it, and the test catches almost all of those. But of the 999,900 healthy people, one in a hundred still gets a wrong positive — that is about ten thousand people, all told they are ill when they are not.

So among everyone who got a positive result, roughly a hundred are ill and ten thousand are fine. Getting a positive moved you from very unlikely to still-quite-unlikely. The test was not bad. Something rare simply stays rare, even after decent evidence.

The general lesson is that a piece of evidence never tells you the answer on its own. It updates whatever you believed beforehand. Start from 'almost nobody has this' and one test will not carry you all the way.

That is the whole of Bayesian thinking: hold a belief, meet evidence, move — by an amount that depends on how strong the evidence is AND how likely the thing was to begin with. Doctors, spam filters, and search-and-rescue teams all run on this, and so does anyone who changes their mind well.

aha.title: Rare things need stronger evidence
aha.text: The rarer something is, the more convincing a result has to be before you should believe it. This is why one surprising study rarely settles anything, and why the reply 'that would be extraordinary, so I want better proof' is good reasoning rather than stubbornness.

aha.title: It tells you how much to move, not what to think
aha.text: Two sensible people can see the same evidence and end up in different places, because they started in different places. The rule does not fix your starting belief. It fixes how far the evidence should shift it.

aha.title: You already do this
aha.text: A friend says they saw a fox in the garden and you believe them instantly. They say they saw a tiger and you ask questions. Same friend, same reliability — different starting odds. That reflex, written down carefully, is the entire subject.

preface.closer: Evidence does not replace what you believed. It moves it.
